developments.title: Grok Bot Galaxy livestream starts
detail: Lauren Tan and Matt Palmer began the Grok Bot Galaxy livestream, a live broadcast exploring rapid company building in three days.
The stream is hosted on Luma and is currently live, allowing viewers to follow the process in real time.
developments.why_it_matters: The livestream provides immediate insight into rapid AI‑driven product development, showcasing practical techniques for building a company quickly.

developments.title: Anubis proof-of-work challenge bypassed by Codex on Lobsters
detail: Lobsters experienced a broken Anubis rollout that prevented users from upvoting or messaging site moderators.
Anubis is a proof-of-work challenge system intended to deter automated AI scrapers from accessing a site.
According to the report, Codex was able to solve the Anubis challenge and send a message to the moderators despite the broken rollout, while regular users could not.
developments.why_it_matters: The report indicates that an automated system can solve the Anubis challenge, which directly undermines the proof-of-work mechanism's ability to block AI scrapers on sites that rely on it.

developments.title: Run Two Codex Accounts Simultaneously on macOS
detail: Edi Hasaj published a step‑by‑step guide for macOS that creates a second Codex (ChatGPT Work) profile, giving it its own Dock icon and launcher. The process involves loading the blog post, launching the secondary account, confirming login with a short agent reply, and then using Spotlight or Raycast shortcuts to switch between the two instances.

With this setup users can keep two distinct Codex sessions active at the same time, allowing independent workflows—such as separating personal and work prompts—without repeatedly logging out and back in.
developments.why_it_matters: The ability to run two Codex accounts concurrently on a single Mac lets developers maintain separate contexts and increase productivity without needing multiple machines or constant re‑authentication.

external_links.title: How to Run Two Codex Accounts on macOS with Separate Profiles | Edi Hasaj

developments.title: Exein raises $270M at $1.7B valuation to secure AI-to-physical interfaces
detail: Exein, a cybersecurity company that secures the interface between AI and physical systems such as robots, drones, autonomous vehicles, and industrial machines, raised $270M at a $1.7B valuation, according to Daniel Miessler.
Miessler reports that Exein's software currently runs on more than two billion devices and that its network observes roughly 5,000 new attacks per week, about 5x the volume seen a year ago.
developments.why_it_matters: Pairing a $1.7B valuation with reported 5x year-over-year attack growth signals that AI-to-physical integrations are an active, recognized attack surface, with Exein now among the better-capitalized vendors tasked with defending them.

developments.title: OpenClaw adds “Fly” skill to ClawHub
detail: OpenClaw announced a new skill for its ClawHub platform that enables a virtual “fly” to make choices between user‑provided options. Users can terminate the fly with the Bugasalt command.

The skill, demonstrated by newcomer McBain, expands ClawHub’s automation capabilities, allowing developers to script decision‑making processes and integrate simple interactive agents. Installation instructions are provided via a linked repository.
developments.why_it_matters: The addition lets developers quickly prototype decision‑making bots within ClawHub, broadening the platform’s automation use cases.

developments.title: typesafeainate releases dspy-typesafeify decorator for dspy Signatures
detail: typesafeainate published the dspy-typesafeify repository on GitHub, which adds a decorator for dspy Signatures that automatically uses TypeSafe where relevant.
The decorator gives dspy users a way to apply TypeSafe to their signatures without manually configuring each one.
developments.why_it_matters: It provides dspy developers an automated way to add TypeSafe checking to their Signatures without per-signature manual configuration.

developments.title: Diogo Almeida launches Jev, a frontier model trained with RLCD
detail: Diogo Almeida announced the release of Jev, a frontier AI model he says was trained with a new method called Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD), which he developed over two years in stealth.

According to the announcement, Jev is optimized for composable intelligence aimed at decisions rather than chat, with claimed performance of 20-200x faster and 40-400x cheaper than comparable frontier models, plus free output tokens. The speed and cost figures are self-reported in the launch announcement.
developments.why_it_matters: Jev makes a decision-optimized frontier model available now at the announced 20-200x-faster, 40-400x-cheaper price point, and RLCD enters the field as a named training method.

developments.title: Mark Zuckerberg cites Meta's months-long Muse delay as evidence that voluntary, self-administered safety measures should guide AI labs rather than collective constraints
detail: Mark Zuckerberg published an essay arguing that the right path to a safe AI future is for each lab to take its own safety actions rather than wait for collective or governmental rules, because doing so is already in each lab's interest, citing market pull for alignment (users will not adopt misaligned agents), significant liability for harms, engagement of independent evaluators and advisors as adoptable best practice, and Meta's commitment of the significant majority of its compute to serving people rather than racing toward recursive self-improvement — a balance of power he frames as within reach.

As part of this framing, Meta delayed shipping its Muse model for several months citing a focus on safety and security, presented as internal, day-to-day responsibility rather than a coordinated industry call, leaving Muse unavailable to users and developers during the delay while Meta strengthens security foundations and aligns the model with emerging safety standards.
Both elements are reported rather than independently verified.
developments.why_it_matters: One of the largest AI labs has publicly endorsed voluntary, self-administered safety measures over binding collective limits, and its multi-month Muse delay is presented as evidence that such steps are operationally feasible — a concrete position that shifts the industry coordination debate while pushing back Muse's availability.
